current_answer: A controlled hiring-and-investor-pitch experiment found that ChatGPT-assisted text made prior expertise harder to judge on average: pooled screening accuracy fell by 4–9%. In a non-English-speaking subgroup, accuracy improved instead. The exercises did not measure real job offers, hires, wages or employment. A separate cover-letter study reported better letters but no increase in its interview-invitation outcome. Separate U.S. occupation data still show rising posted pay alongside lower pay for workers who stayed, while narrow entry-level warnings and a broad no-clear-footprint monitor cover different outcomes. No study here predicts one person’s job risk.

catalogue_card.question: Did AI-written pitches make hiring harder to judge?
catalogue_card.text: In a controlled hiring-and-investor-pitch test, ChatGPT-assisted text reduced accuracy in identifying prior experience on average. The study did not measure real hires, and some non-English-speaking writers saw the opposite result.

summary: A controlled 2023 experiment found a 4–9% pooled screening-accuracy loss when pitch writers could use ChatGPT.
The direction reversed for writers from non-English-speaking contexts.
A separate peer-reviewed cover-letter study reports better written applications but no increase in its interview-invitation outcome.
The exercise measured judgments about experience, not real applications, job offers, wages or employment.
uncertainty: The new 4–9% estimate pools hiring and startup-investing simulations, not actual recruitment outcomes.
Only the official abstract and university summary of the separate cover-letter study were accessible; full methods and invitation measure were not verified.
The no-AI draft always came before the AI-assisted draft, and reviewers knew when AI was available; real-world use and evaluation may differ.
The wage and early-career studies do not identify one common causal AI effect, and broad U.S. indicators can miss narrow changes.
freshness_note: Checked 29 September 2026. Added controlled screening evidence; actual hiring effects remain unmeasured.
